overview.text: An inverse is a mathematical partner that reverses an operation or transformation: applying an operation and then its inverse returns the starting value. For functions, if f(a)=b, then f⁻¹(b)=a; composing the two in either order gives the identity, where defined. A function has an inverse function only when it is one-to-one, meaning different inputs have different outputs; restricting its domain can sometimes make this possible. For a square matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹=A⁻¹A=I, with I the identity matrix. A matrix inverse exists exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Function notation f⁻¹ means “inverse function,” not 1/f.

key_facts.text: For an invertible function, input-output pairs switch: if f(a)=b, then f⁻¹(b)=a. The compositions f⁻¹∘f and f∘f⁻¹ return the original input where defined.
A function must be one-to-one to have an inverse function; on a graph, this is tested with the horizontal line test.
The full function f(x)=x² is not one-to-one, but restricting its domain to x≥0 gives it the inverse f⁻¹(x)=√x.
A matrix inverse is defined for a square matrix A by the two checks AA⁻¹=I and A⁻¹A=I; I has ones on its main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not zero; if the determinant is zero, it has no inverse.
For a nonzero number a, its multiplicative inverse is its reciprocal, 1/a; zero has no multiplicative inverse.

sources.supports: Defines a number’s multiplicative inverse and a matrix inverse; explains the identity matrix and the conditions AA⁻¹=I and A⁻¹A=I.

sources.title: 3.2: Determinants and Matrix Inverses
sources.supports: States the determinant criterion: a square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero.
